toth-arpad-promenade.description: A tree-lined walk along the castle wall in Buda Castle District, laid out on the line of an old defensive passage. It looks out toward the Buda hills, Tabán and Gellért Hill, carries the name of the poet Árpád Tóth, and is known for the Japanese ornamental cherries that bloom along it in spring.
paragraphs: The Tóth Árpád Promenade (Tóth Árpád sétány) runs along the castle wall on the western side of the Buda Castle District. Time Out Budapest describes it as a route with centuries of history that began as a defensive passage and later became a walkway. Today it is a quiet, green stretch of the district that most visitors use as a slow alternative to the busier squares around Matthias Church.

The views are the main reason to come. Visit Buda Castle speaks of vistas toward the Buda hills and the city, while Time Out highlights the outlook over the Tabán district and Gellért Hill. In spring, Japanese ornamental cherry trees blossom along the path, and both sources single this season out as the most photogenic time to walk it.

The name is more recent than the walkway. According to a Hungarian city-culture article, the area behind the castle wall was occupied by gardens until 1936, when they were cleared and the Bástya sétány (Bastion Promenade) was created. In the second half of the 1960s that promenade was divided into sections, and the Tóth Árpád sétány is one half of the former Bástya sétány. It is named after the poet Árpád Tóth (1886-1928), a lyric poet associated with the Nyugat circle; the Castle District heritage site says the lane received its present name in 1946. None of the pages consulted explains why he was chosen.

Along the walk you can find a statue of Artúr Görgei at the Fehérvári rondella, according to Time Out, and the promenade is within a few minutes of Dísz tér, the Vienna Gate (Bécsi kapu) and the Fisherman's Bastion. Visit Buda Castle also places it near Kapisztrán tér and the Military History Institute and Museum, which makes it an easy addition to a Castle District day.
tips: Spring, when the ornamental cherry trees bloom, is the season both Time Out and Visit Buda Castle recommend for the promenade.
Time Out suggests starting at the Castle, walking down toward Tabán and finishing near Gellért Hill.
Dísz tér, the Vienna Gate and the Fisherman's Bastion are all a few minutes' walk away, so the promenade combines well with a Castle District visit.

garden-of-philosophers.description: A small sculpture garden on the side of Gellért Hill, where eight life-size bronze figures by Nándor Wagner face a shared centre. Religious founders and thinkers stand together in a work meant to show what cultures have in common. It was a gift from the sculptor's widow and was unveiled in 2001.
paragraphs: The Garden of Philosophers (Filozófusok kertje) is a quiet sculpture group on the western side of Gellért Hill, between Orom utca and Hegyalja út and behind the Rudas Baths. It is the work of the sculptor Nándor Wagner, and Visit Buda Castle describes it as an eight-figure group that highlights values which religions and cultures share. The life-size bronze figures face each other, looking toward the geometric centre of the group.

A guide from the XpatLoop site names the figures. Five stand in a ring around a sunken pool: Abraham, Jesus, Buddha, Laozi and Akhenaten. Abraham is the only one not standing, and crouches with his head in his hands. Behind the ring stand Mahatma Gandhi, Bodhidharma and Saint Francis of Assisi. Each figure focuses on a small globe, which the guide says represents divine essence. Wikipedia describes Wagner's wider concept as having a further ring of lawgivers, but the Budapest sources describe eight figures, which is what stands here.

Wagner was born in Oradea in 1922 and left Hungary after the 1956 revolution, living first in Sweden and then in Japan, where he died in 1997. According to Wikipedia he conceived the work in Mashiko, Japan, as a spiritual message for future generations. The Budapest set was a gift from his widow and was unveiled on Gellért Hill on 18 October 2001. XpatLoop adds that the architect István Makk, who had known Wagner and visited him in Japan in 1995, chose the site.

The group has had a difficult history. Hungarian magazine HVG reported in 2007 that three of the bronzes, depicting Gandhi, Saint Francis and Bodhidharma (named Dharma in the article), had been stolen after an earlier attempt the previous October that damaged the figures. The article notes that plaster moulds for recasting exist in Japan. Közterkép and a Budapest city blog report that the three figures were later recast from moulds provided by Wagner's widow and that the full set of eight was back in place by 2010. A separate small sculpture of Prince Buda and Princess Pest stands nearby.
tips: The garden lies on a hillside between Orom utca and Hegyalja út, behind the Rudas Baths, so expect an uphill walk from the riverside.
Three figures were stolen in 2007, but they were recast and the full set of eight was back in place by 2010, and a 2023 guide describes all eight.
It combines naturally with a visit to the Rudas Baths and the other sights on Gellért Hill.

new-york-cafe.description: A Belle Époque coffeehouse on the ground floor of the former New York Life Insurance building on the Grand Boulevard. Its frescoed ceilings, gilded stucco and sixteen carved fauns draw visitors, and for decades writers and poets treated it as an informal office. Today it sits inside a hotel.
paragraphs: The New York Café occupies the ground floor of what was built as the Budapest office of the New York Life Insurance Company, at Erzsébet körút 9-11 on the Grand Boulevard. Wikipedia gives the opening date of the building as 23 October 1894 and names Alajos Hauszmann, Flóris Korb and Kálmán Giergl as its architects. The company's name explains the name of the café, and the building is now the Anantara New York Palace Budapest Hotel.

The café became known for its interior, which visitors describe as frescoed ceilings, gilded stucco panels, marble columns and large chandeliers. Wikipedia credits the sculptor Károly Senyei with the statues and ornaments of the facade and with the café's sixteen devilish fauns. It also describes the café as a longtime centre of Hungarian literature and poetry, and a travel guide notes that writers used it as an informal office for working, meeting colleagues and finding patrons.

The twentieth century was less kind. The building was damaged in the Second World War and later nationalised under communism. In 1954 the café was renamed the Hungaria Café, and in 1957 the sculptors Sándor Boldogfai Farkas, Ödön Metky and János Sóváry carved replicas of the damaged allegorical sculptures, among them figures of Thrift and Wealth and of America and Hungary. The café regained its New York name in 1989, after the fall of communism.

In early 2001 the Hungarian government sold the building to the Italian hotel group Boscolo, and after a complete renovation it reopened as a hotel on 5 May 2006 with the restored café. The hotel changed names several times and has been called Anantara New York Palace Budapest since November 2021. For visitors, the café is on the Grand Boulevard near Blaha Lujza tér, and because it sits inside a hotel it is worth confirming current access and any booking arrangements on the official site.
tips: Metro line M2 and trams 4 and 6 are listed by one guide as the way to reach the area around Blaha Lujza tér on the Grand Boulevard.
Look up at the ceilings and for the carved fauns, which Wikipedia attributes to Károly Senyei.
The café is part of a hotel, so check the official site for current opening times, access and any reservation rules.

cafe-gerbeaud.description: A confectionery founded in 1858 that moved to Vörösmarty Square in 1870 and took its name from the Swiss-born confectioner Emil Gerbeaud. Marble, exotic woods and Rococo-style stucco shaped the interior, and the café survived nationalisation under another name before the Gerbeaud name returned in 1984.
paragraphs: Café Gerbeaud stands on Vörösmarty Square in downtown Pest and is one of the best-known coffeehouses in Budapest. Gerbeaud's own timeline says the confectioner Henrik Kugler opened a café-confectionery on 14 October 1858 at what is now József nádor Square, and that he moved to today's Vörösmarty Square in 1870. Wikipedia says the new premises were on the ground floor of the head office of the Hungarian Commercial Bank of Pest, when the square was still called Gizella Square.

The name comes from Emil Gerbeaud, a Swiss confectioner who gained experience in Germany, France and England. Kugler had no successor and met Gerbeaud in Paris in 1882. Gerbeaud came to Budapest as a partner, gradually took over the shop and kept the original name. He introduced products such as butter creams, Parisian creams and many tea pastries. Wikipedia reports that by the end of 1899 he employed about 150 people, and Gerbeaud's own timeline notes that he served on the juries of world fairs in Brussels and Paris and received the French Legion of Honour.

The interior owes much to a 1910 design with advice from Henrik Darilek, who mainly used marble, exotic woods and bronze, according to Wikipedia. The ceiling stucco is in the Rococo style of Louis XV, the chandeliers were inspired by Empress Maria Theresa, and the café had French and Secessionist tables bought at the Paris world fair. Wikipedia lists Ferenc Deák, Franz Liszt and Empress Elisabeth among its guests.

Emil Gerbeaud died on 8 November 1919 and his wife ran the business until 1940. The shop was nationalised in 1948 and renamed Vörösmarty after the poet Mihály Vörösmarty, and the Gerbeaud name returned in 1984. In 1995 a German businessman, Erwin Müller, bought the building, according to the café's timeline, and the interior and offer have been renewed since, most recently in 2025. Váci utca, the pedestrian shopping street, begins at the square, and the Vörösmarty tér station of the M1 metro lies beneath it.
tips: The M1 metro runs under Vörösmarty Square, and Váci utca, the pedestrian shopping street, starts at the square.
Sources disagree on small details, such as whether Gerbeaud arrived in 1884 or a year after meeting Kugler in 1882, so treat exact early dates with care.
Check the official site for current opening times and the seasonal terrace arrangements before you go.

lukacs-thermal-bath.description: A thermal bath in Buda's Felhévíz district whose springs have been used for centuries. Wikipedia traces bathing on the site to at least the 12th century, and the present complex developed from the 1880s onward. Over time it became a favourite of Hungarian writers, composers and filmmakers, and it still has a medical side.
paragraphs: The Lukács Bath (Szent Lukács gyógyfürdő) lies on the Buda side in the 2nd district, in an area the Middle Ages called Felhévíz, a name that refers to its thermal springs. Wikipedia says thermal baths have been used on the site since at least the 12th century, by the Knights Hospitaller. During the Ottoman period the spring water powered a mill, and a wall inside the bath is described as a remnant of the Ottoman Császár powder mill.

The present bath grew from development that began in the mid-1880s. A Hungarian cultural article says Palotay bought the area from the treasury in 1884 and named it Szent Lukács, Saint Luke, after which the bath became a public limited company in 1893, with a mud bath, spa hotel and public steam bath. Rezső Ray the elder designed the hotel, and Rezső Hikisch unified the facade in a Classicist-Biedermeier style in the 1920s. A drinking-cure hall was built in 1937, during the First International Congress of Bathing.

Lukács was well known across the Monarchy and Europe, and until the Széchenyi and Gellért baths were completed it was Budapest's most significant thermal bath. Budappest, a travel site, names the composer Zoltán Kodály as a regular guest and the writers Gyula Illyés and Tibor Déry and the filmmakers Károly Makk and Péter Bacsó as notable patrons. In the courtyard and walls are gratitude plaques left by visitors who felt healed. Many were lost in the Second World War, and the surviving ones were built into the walls during renovation.

After the war a hospital moved into the former hotel, and the National Institute of Rheumatology has operated there since 1951, which is why Lukács still combines medical treatment with bathing. Wikipedia lists thermal pools of different temperatures, swimming pools, a wellness section, sauna facilities and a gallery. A restoration completed in 2013 is reported to have received an ICOMOS award. Across Frankel Leó út is the Malom Lake area, where a building known as the Turkish bath was never Turkish at all, but a people's steam bath built by Palotay.
tips: The bath's official site lists trams 4, 6, 17 and 19, buses 9 and 109 and the HÉV suburban railway (Margit híd stop) as ways to reach it; check BKK's journey planner for the best route to Frankel Leó út 25-29.
Facilities, sauna rules and which pools are available differ by section, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and rules.
Look for the gratitude plaques in the walls and the drinking-cure hall from 1937.

rudas-thermal-bath.description: A Buda bath beside Erzsébet Bridge whose Ottoman core, an octagonal pool under a dome on eight columns, dates from the 16th century. Later wings add a swimming pool and a modern wellness area. Its gender-separated apron bathing was added to Hungary's national intangible heritage list in October 2026.
paragraphs: The Rudas Baths stand at Döbrentei tér 9 on the Buda bank, at the foot of Gellért Hill beside Erzsébet Bridge. Wikipedia describes it as founded in 1571 or 1572 under Ottoman rule, when Sokollu Mustafa Pasha, the governor of Buda, commissioned it. Other sources give a work period of 1566 to 1572 for converting the earlier building, so the exact dates vary by source. A guide from We Love Budapest adds that Hospitaller knights had built a hospital and a bath on the site under King Béla IV.

The Ottoman core is the main thing to see. An octagonal pool lies under a hemispherical dome supported by eight columns, with small windows letting in light. A 2012 article gives the dome a diameter of about ten metres. The Ottoman-period name, Jesil Direkli ilidzsa, is translated as green-columned bath, though We Love Budapest notes that archaeologists have never found the green column, and offers one theory that the later name Rudas comes from a Serbian and Bosnian shortening meaning mineral-water bath.

The complex grew in stages. Xpatloop reports that the swimming pool was built in 1896 and that from 1936 the thermal bath was visited exclusively by men. A 19th-century classicist wing houses an indoor pool, and the Juventus wing, on the site of a former mineral-water bottling plant, opened in 2014 as a modern wellness area with a facade of girih patterns. Wikipedia notes a comprehensive interior renovation that ended with a reopening at the beginning of 2006.

Rudas also carries a social tradition. A Time Out report dated 20 October 2026 says that the gender-separated bathing in cotton aprons was added to the National Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage, and that the listing protects the practice, not the building. Visitors should check the official site for which days are single-sex and which are mixed, because those arrangements have changed over time. Wikipedia also records that the opening scene of the 1988 film Red Heat was filmed here.
tips: The bath's official site lists trams 19, 41, 56 and 56A and several bus lines as ways to reach Döbrentei tér; check BKK's journey planner for the best route.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and the schedule of men's, women's and mixed days, which have changed over time.
The baths stand at the foot of Gellért Hill, so the hill is close by for a walk before or after your visit.

palatinus-bath.description: Budapest's first outdoor beach on Margaret Island, opened in 1919 and expanded in the 1930s with a modernist changing building and a wave pool. Its thermal-well water, historic mosaics and year-round indoor wellness section, added in a 2017 reconstruction, make it one of the city's most layered bathing complexes.
paragraphs: The Palatinus Strandfürdő is a bathing complex on Margaret Island, fed by the island's thermal wells. According to We Love Budapest it opened on 15 June 1919 as Budapest's first outdoor beach, and Hungarian Wikipedia places the first opening in the era of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, before the Danube embankment had walls. It closed after a year for construction, and the new bath opened permanently in August 1921 with a large main pool and further cold and warm pools.

The best-known building was added in 1937, when the elder István Janáky and Károly Szőke designed a modernist reception and changing block with terraces and spiral staircases, together with a wave pool. Hungarian Wikipedia lists the architectural style as Bauhaus, and the Budapest Info page for the bath carries the same label in its title. We Love Budapest records that the plan caused public debate and that the architect Virgil Bierbauer defended it in the journal Tér és Forma.

Art and sculpture have always been part of the site. At the entrance stood a sculpture by Géza Csorba and, in the ticket hall, a wall painting by István Pekáry referring to an Ady poem, both damaged or destroyed in the war. The painting was restored in the 2017 reconstruction, and Csorba's work was recarved in the 1960s. The wave pool carries a surrealist mosaic by Endre Bálint, whose style is compared to Miró's. Before the Second World War, the bath's continuous water surface made it Europe's largest outdoor bath, according to We Love Budapest.

The reconstruction of 2016-17, carried out by Archikon, winterised the building and added indoor thermal pools, a sauna section and therapy rooms, so the complex now runs outdoor and indoor sections that are not necessarily available at the same times. A 2025 news report states that the indoor section stays open year-round while the outdoor pools work only in the warm season. The wave machine, a piston-driven one, was renovated in 2026, and only a few such machines remain in Hungary, with Budapest having two, at Palatinus and Gellért.
tips: Outdoor pools and slides are seasonal, while the indoor wellness and thermal section is described as available through the year, so check which parts are running on your date.
Look for the mosaic by Endre Bálint at the wave pool and the Pekáry wall painting in the ticket hall.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and house rules before travelling to Margaret Island.

veli-bej-bath.description: A small Ottoman bath of the 1570s, set inside the grounds of a hospital in Buda's 2nd district. A central dome sits over an octagonal pool, the Hospitaller order restored it in the early 2010s, and archaeological finds from the work are on display. It is among the few Ottoman baths in Budapest still in use.
paragraphs: The Veli Bej Bath is a historic Ottoman thermal bath in Budapest's 2nd district, in the Felhévíz area below Rózsadomb. According to Budapest by Locals it was built in 1574-75 by Sokollu Mustafa Pasha, a builder and year the Hospitaller order's own history page also gives, while another Hungarian local-history page says it was completed between 1570 and 1572. Budapest by Locals adds that it survived the recapture of Buda in 1686. The same source calls it the oldest and most beautiful Ottoman bath in Budapest, a superlative that sits uneasily with the Rudas Bath, which Wikipedia dates to 1571 or 1572. A commemorative plaque from its construction is said to remain on a wall.

The building has been changed more than once. In 1806 the bath became the property of the Ordo Hospitalarius, the Hospitaller order that runs the neighbouring hospital. During a reconstruction led by József Hild in 1841-48 it was enlarged and renamed Kaiser Bad, or Császár Fürdő, one source dating the work to 1842. In the 1970s a modern hospital wing was built around the small bath, which is why it is hard to see from the street.

The order later restored the bath with the help of archaeologists and art historians. Sources give 2011 as the completion of the work, while an article from 2018 says it reopened in 2012. Four smaller domed buildings surround a central cupola, and the main pool is octagonal under a traditional Ottoman dome, with four smaller pools around it. Original Ottoman clay pipes found during the work were preserved and can be seen between the pools and the saunas, and a small display holds finds from the excavation.

Modern wellness areas, including saunas and a jacuzzi, were added to the historic core. The bath is run with the hospital, and the sources say admission is regulated, including a limited capacity and an age limit, so check directly before travelling. Its address is Árpád fejedelem útja 7, close to the Margaret Bridge's Buda end, and it sits in the same area as the Lukács and Császár-Komjádi baths.
tips: Budapest by Locals gives trams 4 or 6 to Margit híd Budai hídfő, or trams 17, 19 and 41 to Komjádi Béla utca, as ways to get there.
Admission is regulated, including capacity and age limits, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and rules before going.
Look for the preserved Ottoman clay pipes and the small display of archaeological finds.

aquaworld-resort-budapest.description: A large indoor water park and hotel complex in northern Budapest that opened in December 2008 under a Ramada name. A glass dome 73 metres wide covers the leisure area, which has eleven slides, a wave pool and a surf pool. Check its current name and operator before travelling.
paragraphs: Aquaworld Resort Budapest is a water park and hotel resort in northern Budapest, built around a leisure area under a glass dome. A trade news item from the waterpark supplier Polin says the complex opened in December 2008 as the Ramada Resort - Aquaworld Budapest and calls it Central Europe's largest indoor water theme park. The dome is described as 73 metres wide and 21 metres high.

The same report says the complex included a 261-room hotel and a separate building with 48 apartments. The water park's attractions include a wave pool, a surf pool, a 180-metre mountain river and eleven water slides that together are almost one kilometre long. Six giant slides start from a slide tower next to the dome, reached by a glass lift or stairs, and the highest rides begin from 17 metres up, and a conveyor-type lift returns the tubes to the start. A children's wing has pools of different depths, slides and a playhouse.

A later travel guide describes the resort as one of Europe's largest indoor water theme parks, with a four-star superior hotel, an Oriental Spa and a separate Sauna World. It notes that some outdoor pools are seasonal. The guides disagree on the number of pools: the opening report counts 21, while the later guide gives 17 in one place and 15 in another, so treat any single figure with caution.

The resort lies far from the city centre. The travel guide says public transport is possible but can be tricky, naming buses 30 and 230 from Keleti Railway Station or Heroes' Square, and also mentions a shuttle from Heroes' Square. Because names, operators and arrangements can change, check the official site for the current operating details.
tips: A travel guide lists buses 30 and 230 from Keleti Railway Station or Heroes' Square, and also mentions a shuttle from Heroes' Square, so check the current timetable first.
Slides have height and equipment rules, and some areas such as Sauna World are sold separately, so read the official rules before booking.
Pool counts differ between sources, so check the official site for the current attractions, opening times and tickets.

lupa-beach.description: A sandy beach resort on Lupa Lake, a former quarry in Budakalász, just north of the Budapest city limits. It was developed by Sziget Festival founder Károly Gerendai, who opened it in 2016. The lakeside setting includes watersports and play areas and is seasonal.
paragraphs: Lupa Beach lies on Lake Lupa, in Budakalász, just north of the Budapest city limits. Just Budapest describes the lake as a former quarry transformed into a recreational site, and XpatLoop, writing in 2016, called it a former quarry on the city's northern outskirts where swimming had previously been banned. It is a seasonal destination, so check when it is operating before planning a trip.

The developer was Károly Gerendai, founder of the Sziget Festival. XpatLoop reported that the resort was due to open officially on the evening of 14 July 2016, and that Gerendai described that first summer as a test period to gain experience for the next year. He is reported to have signed a 20-year lease with an option to buy, and as at Sziget the catering and other services were contracted out.

In 2017 the beach was reopened on a larger scale. We Love Budapest reported that the swimmable shoreline had been quadrupled, making the beach about 2.5 kilometres long, and Just Budapest credits Gerendai with the 2017 development. The facilities listed by Just Budapest include a wakeboard centre, kayaking, stand-up paddleboarding, diving, beach volleyball, football, a street-workout park, a children's pool, playgrounds, an inflatable water park and a promenade of food stalls, with accessible pathways.

To get there, Just Budapest suggests the HÉV suburban railway from Batthyány tér toward Budakalász, followed by a walk of about twenty minutes, and says an electric minibus runs from the station to the beach. We Love Budapest names the Budakalász-Lenfonó stop and a summer beach bus. Driving is possible via road 11 toward Szentendre.
tips: Take the HÉV from Batthyány tér toward Budakalász and walk about twenty minutes, or look for the shuttle that Just Budapest says serves the beach.
Lupa Beach is seasonal and outside central Budapest, so check the official site for operating dates, opening times and tickets.
Sources name different HÉV stops (Budakalász and Budakalász-Lenfonó), so confirm your stop before travelling.

romai-open-air-bath.description: A summer-season open-air bath in Óbuda's Rómaifürdő district, on ground that once belonged to Roman Aquincum. The present layout dates from 1964 and was modernised around 2000, with a swimming pool, an adventure pool and several slides. The nearby Danube riverbank is a separate, newer public beach.
paragraphs: The Római Strandfürdő is an open-air bath at Rozgonyi Piroska utca 2 in Óbuda, in Budapest's 3rd district. It is a seasonal summer bath. The BKK listing for the bath describes a large green area in the former Aquincum territory, with a children's pool, a swimming pool and an adventure pool, and the operator's own site is named there for current information.

The bath's name and setting come from the area's past. The BKK listing says the Romans already regarded the local springs as sacred and that chronicles from the time of King Matthias mention a hospital here. These are statements from a listing page, not a full history, so they are best read as local tradition. Hungarian Wikipedia's article on Római-part adds that the neighbourhood of Rómaifürdő sits beside springs where mills once operated in the early 19th century.

The layout seen today dates from a renovation. Programturizmus says the renewed bath opened in 1964 and has kept its layout since, and that in 2000 the three pools were modernised with filtered circulation. The main pool became an adventure pool with a slide, neck showers and bubble jets, and the children's pool became a playground. The slides described include a rafting slide, a steep straight slide, a combined fast-and-winding slide and a family slide that several people can use together.

Do not confuse the bath with the Danube riverbank. According to Telex, a free public Danube beach at Római-part opened in 2021, the first legal one since 1973, but swimming is not allowed there and only wading is. Hungarian Wikipedia says the riverside area was once dominated by boathouses and company holiday resorts. The H5 HÉV line has a stop at Rómaifürdő, the closest rail link named in the sources, though they do not give the walking route.
tips: The H5 Szentendre HÉV stops at Rómaifürdő and Aquincum, according to Hungarian Wikipedia's article on Római-part; check the walking route before you go.
The bath is seasonal, so check the operator's site for current dates, opening times and tickets.
The Danube riverside beach at Római-part is a separate site where swimming is not allowed.
